\[
\begin{gathered}
L_k = G_k - \operatorname{EXPAND}(G_{k+1}),
\qquad
\hat{G}_L = G_L,
\quad
\hat{G}_k = \operatorname{EXPAND}(\hat{G}_{k+1}) + a_k L_k,
\quad
I_{\text{out}} = \hat{G}_0,
\quad
(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3) = (1, 1, 1, 1),
\quad
L = 4,
\qquad
G_{k+1}(i,j) = \sum_{m=-2}^{2} \sum_{n=-2}^{2} w(m)\, w(n)\, G_k(2i+m,\, 2j+n),
\qquad
\operatorname{EXPAND}(G)(i,j) = 4 \sum_{\substack{m,n=-2 \\ i-m,\ j-n \text{ even}}}^{2} w(m)\, w(n)\, G\!\left(\tfrac{i-m}{2},\, \tfrac{j-n}{2}\right),
\qquad
w = \tfrac{1}{16}[1, 4, 6, 4, 1]
\end{gathered}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(G_k\): Level k of the Gaussian pyramid. G_0 is the image.
- \(L_k\): Detail level k of the Laplacian pyramid
- \(a_k\): The gain on detail level k. Levels above 4 keep gain 1.
- \(\hat{G}_k\): The rebuilt level k
- \(w\): The 5-tap kernel [1, 4, 6, 4, 1] / 16
- \(L\): The number of levels

G_0 is the image and G_{k+1} is level k reduced. REDUCE filters level k with the 5-tap kernel w along rows and columns. It keeps every second pixel, starting with the first, so a level of n pixels gives ceil(n / 2). EXPAND goes back up. Each output pixel sums the coarse pixels that land on it, weighted by 2 w(m) along each axis. So a flat level stays flat. Burt and Adelson define w by one number a, with w(0) = a, w(1) = 1/4 and w(2) = 1/4 - a/2. This filter uses a = 0.375, which gives the binomial weights [1, 4, 6, 4, 1] / 16. Each detail level L_k is a level minus the expanded level above it. So it holds the detail that the reduce step removed. Each band holds sizes about twice as large as the band before. The rebuild starts at the top level and adds the detail back one level at a time, each multiplied by its gain a_k. With all gains 1 the image comes back exactly. Gains above 1 boost detail of that size and gains below 1 soften it. The filter is linear, but not shift invariant.
